first_paragraph:
Cloudflare turnstile and challenge page solver in Rust (full reverse, request based)cfsolve is a Rust library and command line tool that solves Cloudflare Turnstile
widgets and challenge pages without a headless browser. It returns a Turnstile
token for widgets or a cf_clearance cookie for challenge pages.Turnstile widgets can be solved using the page URL, the sitekey, and optionally the
page's HTML (this should not be required in most cases).  Challenge pages require a direct
fetch or the HTML of the page.cfsolve impersonates a specific browser, described by a profile file. One is
included: profiles/safari-26-ios.json (Safari on iPhone).Each profile references recorded responses to the challenge's browser checks,
stored as JSON in a directory. Keep each profile with its directory when you
copy. Producing these files requires some manual (or AI) effort though it can
be greatly aided by solving challenges in a real web browser with the proxy
set to the address of a running capture-proxy

title: Breaking the open web won't stop the bad bots (techpolicy.press)

But a journalist anonymously using a crawler to investigate potentially anti-competitive practices by tech companies does not."It does seem like this bill mostly affects normal users and is suspect with more surveillance being pushed. Someone who is using a residential proxy network, headless browsing, and/or TLS fingerprint manipulation to evade rate limits and other controls to issue large volumes of automated requests under a deceptive UserAgent string isn't difficult to describe and differentiate versus a normal user using a UA.The proposed text of the bill is rather straightforward. It turns more on the "stealth" bit than "bot".(a) Prohibition.—A person may not—(1) deploy, direct, or cause to be deployed, a stealth bot to access a website, digital platform, or online service in a manner that is reasonably likely to damage, impair, or burden the technical or commercial operation of a website or other internet service; or(2) intentionally misrepresent, conceal, or obscure the nature of the bot to appear as a human user for use in connection with a generative AI model or service.(6) STEALTH BOT.—The term “stealth bot” means a bot that accesses, retrieves, scans, indexes, scrapes, or otherwise interacts with a website, digital platform, or online service without prior disclosure of its identity and purpose, in particular by—(A) failing to identify itself including through a valid and accurate user-agent string; or(B) failing to disclose the specific nature and purpose of the bot, including any proposed use and purpose of page content (including text and data mining, search indexing, inferencing, artificial intelligence development, support, or operations (such as training, fine tuning, retrieval augmented generation)) or other automated processing at the time access is requested and in a format that the website operator can access.reply

> Someone who is using a residential proxy network, headless browsing, and/or TLS fingerprint manipulation to evade rate limits and other controls to issue large volumes of automated requests under a deceptive UserAgent string isn't difficult to describe and differentiate versus a normal user using a UA.So then why isn't it trying to prohibit making multiple requests from different IP addresses in a residential proxy network, rather than the thing it actually does?> The proposed text of the bill is rather straightforward. It turns more on the "stealth" bit than "bot".Not really, look at the definition of "STEALTH BOT" -- the only thing that nominally distinguishes it from a browser is the word "bot" which isn't itself defined, because the phrase "without prior disclosure of its identity and purpose" is something that a normal web browser doesn't do either.It can't even get it out of it via "a valid and accurate user-agent string", both because that clause says or and it still fails the second one, and because "a valid and accurate user-agent string" is a nonsense phrase. The Safari user agent strings start with "Mozilla" even though it's not. The Android ones do the same and then include "AppleWebKit" and "Mobile Safari" too. A browser extension uses the user agent string of the browser regardless of what the extension does. When Debian packages their version of Firefox, its user agent string says Firefox and not Debian.User agent strings don't have a registry. "Valid" has no meaning and "accurate" is contrary to the default behavior of common browsers.reply

User agent strings are a sad consequence of websites incorrectly parsing them to enable functionality, resulting in a "every bug becomes a contract" type of situation.That being said, if you include GOOGLEBOT in your 1k long query string, alongside a very long page describing your crawlers, how to identify them, how to block them and how to set limits, no judge will find you guilty of concealing your purpose.As for why the law is written as is instead of banning more specific functionality, it's so assholes don't get any ideas on how to bypass it.reply

> User agent strings are a sad consequence of websites incorrectly parsing them to enable functionality, resulting in a "every bug becomes a contract" type of situation.Which is precisely why trying to legislate them is folly. Obviously the reason Android calls itself "Mobile Safari" is so that servers send it the mobile version of the site instead of the desktop one etc.Which makes "accurate" an unreasonable requirement, since there is already a preexisting non-waivable requirement for inaccurate. When someone is making their "turn a web page into a PDF so you can view it later on the plane" software or whatever, it has to use a user agent string that will cause the site to send the version you need turned into the PDF.> That being said, if you include GOOGLEBOT in your 1k long query string, alongside a very long page describing your crawlers, how to identify them, how to block them and how to set limits, no judge will find you guilty of concealing your purpose.First, you're assuming that the person being prosecuted is the entities who are the nominal targets of the bill, when the real problem is when they're not. Because you're proposing a law that says anybody with an inaccurate user agent string is in violation, meanwhile everybody has an inaccurate user agent string.Moreover, consider what you expect the outcome of legislating something like this is going to be. Sites could then try to either blacklist or whitelist user agents.If they do the first one, that doesn't work, because the scraping service can change it whenever they want.If they do the second one, that doesn't work, because now every third party has to start pretending to be a common browser even when they're doing something totally innocent or they get blocked by default for being something else. Which makes the user agent string even less useful than it is now, and subjects innocent parties to arbitrarily liability for doing something they have to do or their client is broken.> As for why the law is written as is instead of banning more specific functionality, it's so assholes don't get any ideas on how to bypass it.You're describing an autocracy. The way you make it so that you always prosecute someone is to make it so that you can always prosecute anyone, which is very bad.reply

> User agent strings are a sad consequence of websites incorrectly parsing them to enable functionality, resulting in a "every bug becomes a contract" type of situation.It's a bit old but https://webaim.org/blog/user-agent-string-history/ is always a good parable.reply
You're slicing the meaning of UA strings too fine.Bots can easily identify themselves through REP in RFC 9309. This isn't difficult or confusing.reply

They came with a legitimate grievance. Newsrooms are being hit by a surge of automated traffic, mostly from AI developers. AI developers extract enormous volumes of online content and then potentially deprive website owners of referral traffic and ad revenue with generative AI features and chatbots trained on that content. It is a real problem that deserves a real solution. But this bill doesn’t directly target the harms caused by abusive crawling. Instead, it would force anyone accessing a website automatically to identify themselves and their purposes for collecting public information. Rather than protect journalists, the bill threatens a basic tool they, and many others, rely on to gather information online.Cutting-edge investigative journalism relies on automated data collection

title: Show HN: A working Nintendo in ~1GB of Qwen weights (github.com/dbreunig)
comments: A couple thoughts on the process here…First off, Opus 5.5 built working weights and code with only two prompts:1. Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.It returned charts well illustrating any model would be _slow_. But it's still fun, so the second prompt was:2. I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.Now while this was an _epic_ run by Opus (5.5 is a crazy capable model), this is a surprisingly well-structured challenge.There is a long-lived and incredible community of classic gaming emulation work online for it to reference. And that community has created…conformance tests! title: sanstun: A sans-IO, parallel-friendly WireGuard implementation in Rust (firezone.dev)
comments: It was all going great until I read> The design also avoids problems like function coloring and plays well with Rust's ownership rules.Async is not I/O. It can be used for I/O, but it's just a way of writing pure, deterministic state machines that keeps a logical flow together instead of scattered over a bunch of transitions.Even if you choose to manually compile your async flows into explicit state machines, you still have to deal with ‘function colouring’ (a.k.a. typing): a flow that crosses several state transitions (and may have other disjoint parts of the state updated in the meantime, via other transitions) now has to be rewritten as a (series of) state transitions, and can't be called from a blocking function. If anything, rewriting all your state machines without `async` makes the function colouring ‘problem’ worse, because multi-transition flows are even more different from normal functions.reply

In principle, you are right. Async is not I/O. And yes, `async` functions compile to a deterministic state machine.The problem is, the moment you use `async`, your state machine reduces down to one API: `poll`. What if I want to change some state in-between two state transitions (i.e. between two `await` points)? Now I have to wire-in a channel to supply that data at the right point or access some shared data via a Mutex.Rust's `async` implementation is great if you know everything upfront before you kick off your state machine. The moment you need to do many things concurrently, it can become a real mess.Firezone's sans-IO core handles many things concurrently: inbound IP, inbound UDP, WebSocket control messages, TURN allocations, timers, user commands, etc. Having essentially one big struct that I can just call `&mut self` functions on for any one of these inputs makes this very easy to understand, compose and test.A few things like TURN request-response handshakes might be easier as an `async` function but in reality, it is not a big deal and the composability you get from it outweighs it in my opinion.reply
Isn't this the idea behind generalizing `async` to `Generator`? You can set the `R` type parameter to whatever type you want to resume the computation with.reply

Sweet, this is basically how I design my protocol implementations in rust as well.Way more testable, the bulk can be shared between async and blocking IO, it's a lot easier to completely ban unsafe in your dependencies (excepting std and core), etc.reply

first_paragraph:
Today, we are announcing sanstun: a sans-IO Rust implementation of the WireGuard® state machine, optimized for ease of use, security and performance through a parallel-friendly and idiomatic API.sans-IO is the idea that you design your system such that IO and side-effects are cleanly separated from the state and "business logic".
The IO in sans-IO doesn't just mean file or network IO.
It also includes things like time and randomness!Due to their lack of side-effects, sans-IO components compose very well and are relatively easy to test.
The design also avoids problems like function coloring and plays well with Rust's ownership rules.The code examples and references in this post are in Rust but sans-IO isn't Rust-specific at all.
Its patterns and ideas can be applied in any language.
For a more in-depth explanation, our sans-IO post is a good place to start.When we first built Firezone, we reached for boringtun as our WireGuard implementation.

title: Jules Verne's Lost Novel (blue-continuum.com)
comments: As mentioned elsewhere in this thread, this book is quite poorly written. But I think it's still enjoyable, in part because you can see the hand of the author pulling the strings so much that it becomes funny. I read an annotated version with context and comments from Verne's editor, and would recommend you to do the same if you're curious.As an example, there's an entire chapter dedicated to Michel and his professor friend going through a long list of nineteenth-century authors and passing judgment on them. You would expect this to be the thinly disguised opinions of Jules Verne, but no, it's the thinly disguised opinions of Verne's editor, which Verne included in the hopes that it would help the book get published. Obviously, this was not successful.I have a theory about Verne that's strongly based on this book. He is sometimes called a technological visionary, but most of the inventions of his books were already known at his time (the first submarine was made in 1620, Around the World in Eighty Days is likely based on an itinerary in a magazine Verne read, etc.), and what was not known, Verne often made work using lots of artistic license (like the giant gun from the Earth to the Moon, which would kill the passengers with the acceleration; Verne did not invent rockets). No, Verne's genius was that he took the progress that was already visible and used it to create adventures, that he created a vision of the future where all this technology is used to explore deep underground caves and the sea floor and outer space and find fascinating things there. And Paris in the Twentieth Century is the negative version of this, a world where technological progress does not expand imagination, but instead limits it, as everything gets economically optimised to death.  It's a good warning to keep in mind.reply
